title: Short Stuff: The Ritchie Boys
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Ritchie Boys, the roughly 20,000 U.S. Army intelligence personnel trained at Camp Ritchie in Maryland during World War Two. The hosts cover who they were (many refugees, including German Jewish refugees and Japanese Americans from internment camps), their eight-week Camp Ritchie training (counterintelligence, aerial photo analysis, interrogation), follow-up training in England, their roles in interrogation, the Red Book (German Army order of battle), and postwar work such as German denazification newspapers and interpreting at the Tokyo war crimes trials. They also discuss the Richie Girls (WAC women, including instructors Sally Davis and Lillian Tombacker), recognition decades later (2022 Eli Wiesel award, a pending Congressional Gold Medal bill), and a possible movie. Some tangents about actors and the show's sign-off are included.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Short Stuff episode and tease the Ritchie Boys topic.

segments.title: Overview of the Ritchie Boys
segments.summary: Roughly 20,000 intelligence officers trained in the US during WWII, about 60 percent American born, including Native American soldiers and about 2,800 German Jewish refugees, plus Japanese Americans who volunteered from internment camps.

segments.title: Camp Ritchie and the Richie Girls
segments.summary: Camp Ritchie began as a National Guard camp in Maryland that the Army took over; the eight-week program included counterintelligence and aerial photo analysis. The WAC women were called Richie Girls. The Guy Ritchie movie joke is made.

segments.title: Language skills, interrogation and the Red Book
segments.summary: After the eight-week course, Ritchie Boys went to England for advanced training and were spread across units. Their language and cultural skills helped interrogations; JD Salinger was among them and was valued for spotting phonies. Hosts say they got about 60 percent of actionable battlefield intelligence and describe the Red Book, a running file on the German Army.
topics: Red Book German Army order of battle

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Posing as Soviet officers to interrogate POWs
segments.summary: German POWs feared handover to the Soviets, so Ritchie Boys reportedly posed as Soviet officers, which made prisoners talkative.

segments.title: Origins of the name and Ernst Kramer
segments.summary: The name Ritchie Boys likely arose after the England training. Ernst Kramer, an 18-year-old German Jewish refugee who survived Buchenwald, became a Ritchie Boy and wrote pamphlets urging German soldiers to surrender and helped set up newspapers.

segments.title: Denazification newspapers and David Akira Tommy
segments.summary: Ritchie Boys ran independent German newspapers in towns during denazification. David Akira Tommy, interned with his family in a US Japanese internment camp, volunteered and became lead interpreter at the Tokyo war crimes trials.

segments.title: Richie Girls instructors and later recognition
segments.summary: Twenty-two women were instructors at Camp Ritchie; Sally Davis and Lillian Tombacker are mentioned, with Tombacker serving as Eisenhower's Polish interpreter and receiving a Bronze Star. The Ritchie Boys were little known until the mid-2000s, received the 2022 Eli Wiesel Award from the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, and a Congressional Gold Medal bill is pending. Sixty-five received Silver Stars.

segments.title: Closing banter and movie talk
segments.summary: Hosts riff on a possible Ritchie Boys movie and actor Benedict Cumberbatch, then wrap up.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts go off script and close the episode with the iHeartRadio production credit.
